stemMd: A mutation changes one codon but the encoded amino acid remains the same. What property of the genetic code permits this?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Several codons can specify the same amino acid.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Amino acids are determined only by the number of chromosomes.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Every codon specifies several amino acids simultaneously.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The ribosome reads DNA directly instead of RNA.

explanationMd: The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are specified by more than one codon. A base substitution can therefore produce a synonymous codon without changing the protein sequence. Degeneracy differs from ambiguity; a codon does not normally instruct several amino acids at once.

distractorRationale.c: The code is normally unambiguous for a given codon in a given context.
distractorRationale.e: The ribosome normally reads messenger RNA.
distractorRationale.b: Translation depends on the codon sequence, not chromosome count.
